title: Units, Dimensions and Measurements
subtitle: Zero-to-JEE-Advanced Visual Textbook: SI Standards, Parallax, Dimensional Analysis, Significant Figures, Error Calculus, Vernier Callipers & Screw Gauge
introduction:
💡 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Is a Measurement?

Suppose someone tells you, “The length of this desk is 5.” Your brain immediately asks: 5 what? 5 meters? 5 feet? 5 pencils?

In Physics, a number by itself is meaningless unless we attach a globally agreed standard reference called a Unit ($u$).

Fundamental Law of Measurement:
Every physical quantity $Q$ is the product of a pure Numerical Value ($n$) and a Standard Unit ($u$). Changing the unit never changes the physical size of the object!
$$\boxed{Q = n \times u = \text{Constant} \implies n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2 \implies n \propto \frac{1}{u}}$$
  • Example: $1\text{ metre} = 100\text{ centimetres}$. Here, the metre is a larger unit ($u_1 > u_2$), so its numerical value is smaller ($1 < 100$).

topics.title: Fundamental, Derived & Supplementary SI Units, Practical Units & Astronomical Parallax
topics.theoryHtml:
1.1 The 7 Fundamental (Base) Quantities of Nature
Fundamental vs. Derived Quantities:
• Fundamental Quantities (7): Independent physical quantities that cannot be expressed in terms of any other physical quantities.
• Derived Quantities: All other quantities (speed, force, energy, voltage, magnetic field) built by multiplying or dividing the 7 base quantities.
No.Base Physical QuantitySI Unit NameSI SymbolDimensional Symbol
1Lengthmetrem$[L]$
2Masskilogramkg$[M]$
3Timeseconds$[T]$
4Electric CurrentampereA$[A]$ or $[I]$
5Thermodynamic TemperaturekelvinK$[K]$ or $[\Theta]$
6Amount of Substancemolemol$[\text{mol}]$
7Luminous Intensitycandelacd$[\text{cd}]$
1.2 The 2 Supplementary SI Units (Plane Angle & Solid Angle)

1. Plane Angle ($d\theta$) — Unit: Radian ($\text{rad}$):
Ratio of circular arc length $ds$ to radius $r$. A full circle subtends $2\pi\text{ rad} = 360^\circ$.

$$\boxed{d\theta = \frac{ds}{r} \text{ rad}} \qquad \left(1^\circ = 60'\text{ (arcmin)}, \; 1' = 60''\text{ (arcsec)}, \; 1'' \approx 4.85 \times 10^{-6}\text{ rad}\right)$$

2. Solid Angle ($d\Omega$) — Unit: Steradian ($\text{sr}$):
The 3D conical angle subtended at the center of a sphere of radius $r$ by a normal surface area patch $dA_{\perp}$. Since the surface area of a complete sphere is $4\pi r^2$, the total 3D solid angle around a point is $4\pi\text{ sr}$.

$$\boxed{d\Omega = \frac{dA_{\perp}}{r^2} \text{ sr}} \qquad \left(\Omega_{\text{complete sphere}} = \frac{4\pi r^2}{r^2} = 4\pi\text{ sr}\right)$$

topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1: Astronomical Parallax Method for Distance of Stars & Planets

Intuition: Hold a pen in front of your face and view it with your left eye, then your right eye. The pen shifts against the distant wall! The distance between your two observation points is the Basis ($b$), and the angular shift is the Parallax Angle ($\theta$).

Step 1: Observe a planet $S$ at distance $D$ simultaneously from two observatories $A$ and $B$ on Earth separated by baseline $b = AB$.

Step 2: Because $D \gg b$, the ratio $b/D \ll 1$, so the baseline $b$ acts as a circular arc of radius $D$:

$$\boxed{\theta \text{ (in radians)} = \frac{\text{Baseline }(b)}{\text{Distance }(D)} \implies D = \frac{b}{\theta}}$$

Step 3 (Linear Diameter $d$ of a Planet): Once $D$ is known, if the planet's disk subtends an angular diameter $\alpha$ (in radians) in a telescope:

$$\boxed{d = D \cdot \alpha}$$
Derivation 2: 3D Solid Angle of a Cone with Semi-Vertical Angle α

Consider a cone of half-angle $\alpha$ cut from a sphere of radius $R$. Slice the spherical cap into thin rings at angle $\theta$ of radius $R\sin\theta$ and strip width $R\,d\theta$:

$$dA = (2\pi R\sin\theta)(R\,d\theta) = 2\pi R^2 \sin\theta\,d\theta$$

Divide by $R^2$ and integrate from $\theta = 0$ to $\theta = \alpha$:

$$\Omega = \int_0^\alpha \frac{2\pi R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta}{R^2} = 2\pi[-\cos\theta]_0^\alpha \implies \boxed{\Omega = 2\pi(1 - \cos\alpha)\text{ sr}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Putting Arcminutes or Arcseconds Directly into $D = b/\theta$): You must convert $\theta$ into radians before dividing! Memorize these three conversion factors:
    • $1^\circ = \frac{\pi}{180}\text{ rad} \approx 1.745 \times 10^{-2}\text{ rad}$
    • $1' = \left(\frac{1}{60}\right)^\circ \approx 2.91 \times 10^{-4}\text{ rad}$
    • $1'' = \left(\frac{1}{3600}\right)^\circ \approx 4.85 \times 10^{-6}\text{ rad}$
  • Trap 2 (Dimensionless vs. Unitless): Plane angle ($\text{rad}$) and Solid angle ($\text{sr}$) have units, but they are dimensionless ($[M^0 L^0 T^0]$). Thus, a dimensionless quantity can have a unit, but a unitless quantity can never have dimensions!

topics.title: Dimensional Formulae, Principle of Homogeneity, 3 Core Applications & Custom Base Systems
topics.theoryHtml:
2.1 What Are Dimensions & The Principle of Homogeneity?
Definition (Dimensional Formula):
An expression showing which powers of the fundamental quantities $[M, L, T, A, K, \text{mol}, \text{cd}]$ enter into a derived physical quantity.
Principle of Homogeneity of Dimensions:
Two physical quantities can be added, subtracted, or equated if and only if they have the exact same dimensions.
$$\text{If } Y = A + B - C, \quad \text{then} \quad \boxed{[Y] = [A] = [B] = [C]}$$

The Transcendental Function Rule (Very High Frequency in JEE!):
The arguments (inputs) and outputs of all trigonometric, exponential, and logarithmic functions are strictly dimensionless $[M^0 L^0 T^0]$:

$$\text{In } y = A e^{-\alpha t} \sin(\omega t - kx): \qquad [\alpha t] = [\omega t] = [kx] = [M^0 L^0 T^0] \quad \text{and} \quad [y] = [A]$$

2.3 Limitations of Dimensional Analysis
  • 1. Cannot find dimensionless constants: It cannot tell whether the numeric factor in kinetic energy is $\frac{1}{2}mv^2$, $3mv^2$, or $2\pi mv^2$.
  • 2. Cannot derive formulas containing sums or differences: It can check $s = ut + \frac{1}{2}at^2$, but cannot derive the two separate added terms at once.
  • 3. Fails when a quantity in Mechanics depends on more than 3 variables: Since $[M, L, T]$ provide only 3 linear equations, we cannot uniquely solve for 4 unknown powers $(a, b, c, d)$.
  • 4. Fails if chosen base quantities are not independent: For example, $[L, v, T]$ cannot form a valid base system because $v = L/T$ already links them!
topics.derivationHtml:
Application 1: Converting Units Between Two Systems (SI to CGS or Custom Units)

For any quantity with dimensions $[M^a L^b T^c]$, applying $n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2$ gives:

$$\boxed{n_2 = n_1 \left[\frac{M_1}{M_2}\right]^a \left[\frac{L_1}{L_2}\right]^b \left[\frac{T_1}{T_2}\right]^c}$$

Worked Proof (Convert SI Viscosity $1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s}$ into CGS Poise):
Viscosity $\eta$ has dimensions $[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-1}]$ ($a = 1, b = -1, c = -1$):

$$n_2 = 1 \left(\frac{1000\text{ g}}{1\text{ g}}\right)^1 \left(\frac{100\text{ cm}}{1\text{ cm}}\right)^{-1} \left(\frac{1\text{ s}}{1\text{ s}}\right)^{-1} = 1000 \times \frac{1}{100} \times 1 = 10 \implies \boxed{1\text{ Pa}\cdot\text{s} = 10\text{ Poise}}$$
Application 2: Expressing Mass in a Custom Base System [Force F, Velocity V, Time T]

Suppose Force $[F]$, Velocity $[V]$, and Time $[T]$ are chosen as fundamental quantities. Find the dimensional formula of Mass $[M]$:

Step 1: Write $M = F^a V^b T^c$ and substitute standard $[M, L, T]$ dimensions:

$$[M^1 L^0 T^0] = [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]^a [L^1 T^{-1}]^b [T^1]^c = [M^a L^{a+b} T^{-2a-b+c}]$$

Step 2 (Compare exponents):

• Power of $M$: $a = 1$
• Power of $L$: $a + b = 0 \implies b = -1$
• Power of $T$: $-2a - b + c = 0 \implies -2(1) - (-1) + c = 0 \implies c = +1$

$$\boxed{[M] = [F^1 V^{-1} T^1]}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Dimensionally Correct $\neq$ Physically Correct): An equation like $v = u + 10at$ is dimensionally valid, yet physically false. However, any dimensionally incorrect equation is 100% false!
  • Trap 2 (Displacement in the $n^{\text{th}}$ Second $S_n = u + \frac{a}{2}(2n - 1)$): Students often think $S_n$ is dimensionally wrong because $u$ has $[LT^{-1}]$ while $S_n$ looks like $[L]$. In reality, $S_n$ is the displacement per unit time ($1\text{ second}$), and $(2n - 1)$ carries hidden dimension $[T^1]$, so every term has dimensions $[L^1 T^{-1}]$ (or $[L]$ over $1\text{ s}$)!

topics.title: Significant Figures, Rounding-Off Rules, Arithmetic Precision & Order of Magnitude
topics.theoryHtml:
3.1 First-Time Reader Intuition: What Are Significant Figures?
Definition (Significant Figures):
In any measured value, the reliable (certain) digits PLUS the first uncertain (estimated) digit are called Significant Figures (SF). They tell us the precision of the measuring instrument!

The 7 Golden Rules for Counting Significant Figures:

  1. All non-zero digits are significant ($482.6 \to \mathbf{4\text{ SF}}$).
  2. Trapped zeros between non-zero digits are ALWAYS significant ($2005 \to \mathbf{4\text{ SF}}$).
  3. Leading zeros to the left of the first non-zero digit are NEVER significant ($0.0042 \to \mathbf{2\text{ SF}}$).
  4. Trailing zeros WITH a decimal point are ALWAYS significant ($4.500\text{ m} \to \mathbf{4\text{ SF}}$; $0.080\text{ s} \to \mathbf{2\text{ SF}}$).
  5. Trailing zeros WITHOUT a decimal point are NOT significant ($6500 \to \mathbf{2\text{ SF}}$).
  6. Powers of 10 ($\times 10^n$) and unit changes NEVER alter the number of significant figures ($1.20\text{ m} = 120.\text{ cm} = 1.20 \times 10^3\text{ mm} \to$ all have $\mathbf{3\text{ SF}}$).
  7. Exact counting numbers or pure formula constants (like $2$ in $d = 2r$ or $6$ in cube surface area $6a^2$) have infinite ($\infty$) significant figures.
3.2 Rounding-Off Rules (The Even–Odd Rule for Digit 5)
$$\text{When the digit to be dropped is } \mathbf{\text{EXACTLY } 5} \text{ (or } 5 \text{ followed only by zeros):}$$
  • If the preceding digit is EVEN: Leave it unchanged ($4.65 \to \mathbf{4.6}$).
  • If the preceding digit is ODD: Increase it by $1$ so it becomes even ($4.75 \to \mathbf{4.8}$).
  • Note: If the $5$ is followed by ANY non-zero digit (e.g., $4.651$), ALWAYS round up ($4.651 \to \mathbf{4.7}$).
3.3 Algebraic Operations with Significant Figures
OperationMaster RuleWorked Example
Addition & Subtraction ($+$ or $-$)Count Decimal Places (DP) only! Round the final answer to the least number of decimal places among the inputs.$14.28\text{ g}$ (2 DP) $+ 2.1\text{ g}$ (1 DP) $= 16.38\text{ g} \to$ Round to 1 DP $\implies \mathbf{16.4\text{ g}}$.
Multiplication & Division ($\times$ or $\div$)Count Total Significant Figures (SF)! Round the final answer to the least total SF among the inputs.$\text{Density} = \frac{4.237\text{ g } (4\text{ SF})}{2.51\text{ cm}^3\text{ } (3\text{ SF})} = 1.68804\dots \to$ Round to 3 SF $\implies \mathbf{1.69\text{ g/cm}^3}$.
topics.derivationHtml:
How to Find the Order of Magnitude of Any Quantity

Step 1: Express the quantity in scientific notation $N = a \times 10^b$ where $1 \le a < 10$.

Step 2 (Comparison with $\sqrt{10} \approx 3.16$ or $5$):

• If $a \le 5$ (or $a \le 3.16$), the Order of Magnitude is $\mathbf{b}$.
• If $a > 5$ (or $a > 3.16$), approximate $a \approx 10^1$, so the Order of Magnitude is $\mathbf{b + 1}$.

Example: Speed of light $c = 3.0 \times 10^8\text{ m/s} \implies$ Since $3.0 \le 3.16$, Order of Magnitude $= \mathbf{8}$. Mass of electron $m_e = 9.1 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg} = 0.91 \times 10^{-30}\text{ kg} \implies$ Order of Magnitude $= \mathbf{-30}$.

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Confusing Decimal Places with Significant Figures in Addition): When adding $25.4\text{ cm} + 0.082\text{ cm} = 25.482\text{ cm}$, do NOT look at total significant figures! Because $25.4$ has only 1 decimal place, the sum must be rounded to 1 decimal place: $\mathbf{25.5\text{ cm}}$.
  • Trap 2 (Subtraction Destroying Significant Figures): $18.45\text{ cm} - 18.41\text{ cm} = 0.04\text{ cm}$. Both inputs had 4 significant figures (and 2 decimal places), so the result keeps 2 decimal places ($0.04\text{ cm}$) and has only 1 significant figure!

topics.title: Theory of Errors & Calculus-Based Error Propagation (Power Law, Parallel Resistors & Lenses)
topics.theoryHtml:
4.1 Absolute, Mean Absolute, Relative & Percentage Error

Suppose we measure a quantity $n$ times and obtain readings $a_1, a_2, \dots, a_n$:

$$\text{1. True (Mean) Value: } a_m = \frac{a_1 + a_2 + \dots + a_n}{n}$$
$$\text{2. Mean Absolute Error: } \Delta a_m = \frac{|a_m - a_1| + |a_m - a_2| + \dots + |a_m - a_n|}{n}$$
$$\text{3. Relative Error} = \frac{\Delta a_m}{a_m} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \text{4. Percentage Error} = \left(\frac{\Delta a_m}{a_m}\right) \times 100\%$$
Single-Measurement Rule:
If no repeated readings are given, the maximum possible absolute error $\Delta x$ is equal to the Least Count (LC) of the measuring instrument!
4.2 Laws of Maximum Error Propagation

Because individual measurement errors can reinforce one another in the worst case, maximum errors ALWAYS add:

$$\textbf{1. Addition or Subtraction } (Z = A \pm B): \qquad \boxed{\Delta Z = \Delta A + \Delta B}$$
$$\textbf{2. Multiplication or Division } \left(Z = A \cdot B \text{ or } \frac{A}{B}\right): \qquad \boxed{\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = \frac{\Delta A}{A} + \frac{\Delta B}{B}}$$
$$\textbf{3. General Power Formula } \left(Z = \frac{k A^p B^q}{C^r}\right): \qquad \boxed{\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = |p|\frac{\Delta A}{A} + |q|\frac{\Delta B}{B} + |r|\frac{\Delta C}{C}}$$
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1: Why Parallel Resistors Use ΔRp / Rp² = ΔR1 / R1² + ΔR2 / R2²

Warning: Never apply the quotient rule to $R_p = \frac{R_1 R_2}{R_1 + R_2}$ because $R_1$ and $R_2$ appear in both numerator and denominator (they are not independent!). Instead, differentiate the reciprocal equation:

$$R_p^{-1} = R_1^{-1} + R_2^{-1}$$

Differentiating using $\frac{d}{dx}(x^{-1}) = -x^{-2}\,dx$:

$$-\frac{dR_p}{R_p^2} = -\frac{dR_1}{R_1^2} - \frac{dR_2}{R_2^2} \implies \boxed{\frac{\Delta R_p}{R_p^2} = \frac{\Delta R_1}{R_1^2} + \frac{\Delta R_2}{R_2^2} \implies \Delta R_p = R_p^2\left(\frac{\Delta R_1}{R_1^2} + \frac{\Delta R_2}{R_2^2}\right)}$$
Derivation 2: Simple Pendulum Gravity Error with N Oscillations

Since $T = 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{L}{g}}$, squaring gives $g = \frac{4\pi^2 L}{T^2}$. If total time $t$ is measured for $N$ oscillations, then $T = \frac{t}{N}$, so $\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{\Delta t}{t}$:

$$\boxed{\frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\Delta T}{T} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\Delta t}{t}}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Never Subtract Errors in $Z = A - B$!): If $A = (20 \pm 0.2)\text{ cm}$ and $B = (15 \pm 0.1)\text{ cm}$, then $Z = A - B = 5\text{ cm}$, and $\Delta Z = 0.2 + 0.1 = 0.3\text{ cm}$ (NOT $0.2 - 0.1$). Thus $\%\text{ error in } Z = \frac{0.3}{5} \times 100\% = 6\%$.
  • Trap 2 (Large Percentage Changes $> 10\%$): Calculus error formulas like $\frac{\Delta K}{K} = 2\frac{\Delta p}{p}$ work ONLY for small errors ($\le 5\%$). If momentum $p$ increases by $100\%$ ($p' = 2p$), kinetic energy $K \propto p^2$ becomes $4K$, an increase of $\mathbf{300\%}$ (not $200\%$)!

topics.title: Experimental Instruments: Vernier Callipers, Screw Gauge (Micrometer), Spherometer & Zero Errors
topics.theoryHtml:
5.1 Vernier Callipers: Least Count & Reading Formula
How the Vernier Scale Works:
A Vernier scale has divisions ($1\text{ VSD}$) slightly different in width from the Main Scale divisions ($1\text{ MSD}$). The tiny difference between the two is the Least Count (Vernier Constant)!
$$\boxed{\text{Least Count (LC)} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}}$$

If $n$ divisions of the Vernier Scale coincide with $m$ divisions of the Main Scale ($n\text{ VSD} = m\text{ MSD} \implies 1\text{ VSD} = \frac{m}{n}\text{ MSD}$):

$$\boxed{\text{LC} = \left(1 - \frac{m}{n}\right)\text{MSD}} \qquad \left(\text{Standard Case } m = n-1: \; \text{LC} = \frac{1\text{ MSD}}{n}\right)$$
$$\textbf{Complete Vernier Reading:} \quad \boxed{\text{True Reading} = \text{MSR} + (\text{VSR} \times \text{LC}) - (\text{Zero Error})}$$
Zero Error Type (Jaws Closed Empty)Visual ConditionFormula (If $k^{\text{th}}$ VSD coincides out of $N$)Correction Rule
Positive Zero Error ($+\text{ZE}$)Vernier zero ($0_V$) is to the RIGHT of Main Scale zero ($0_M$).$\text{ZE} = +k \times \text{LC}$Subtract $|\text{ZE}|$ from observed reading.
Negative Zero Error ($-\text{ZE}$)Vernier zero ($0_V$) is to the LEFT of Main Scale zero ($0_M$).$\boxed{\text{ZE} = -(N - k) \times \text{LC}}$Add $|\text{ZE}|$ to observed reading.
5.2 Screw Gauge (Micrometer) & Spherometer
Definition (Pitch $p$):
The axial linear distance moved by the screw spindle per one complete rotation ($360^\circ$) of the circular cap.
$$\text{Pitch } (p) = \frac{\text{Distance Moved Along Linear Scale}}{\text{Number of Full Rotations}} \qquad \bigg| \qquad \boxed{\text{Least Count (LC)} = \frac{\text{Pitch }(p)}{\text{Total Circular Divisions }(N)}}$$
$$\textbf{Complete Screw Gauge Reading:} \quad \boxed{\text{True Reading} = \text{PSR} + (\text{CSR} \times \text{LC}) - (\text{Zero Error})}$$
  • Positive Zero Error ($+\text{ZE}$): When studs touch, Circular Scale zero ($0_C$) stays BELOW the reference line. If $k^{\text{th}}$ mark aligns: $\text{ZE} = +k \times \text{LC}$.
  • Negative Zero Error ($-\text{ZE}$): When studs touch, Circular Scale zero ($0_C$) crosses ABOVE the reference line. If $k^{\text{th}}$ mark aligns (out of $N$ divisions): $\boxed{\text{ZE} = -(N - k) \times \text{LC}}$.
  • Backlash Error: Caused by wear and tear (loose play) in screw threads when rotation direction is suddenly reversed. Cure: Always rotate the screw in one single direction while taking a reading!
topics.derivationHtml:
Derivation 1: First-Principles Method for Non-Standard & Retrograde JEE Advanced Verniers

When a JEE Advanced problem gives a non-standard Vernier (e.g., $1\text{ VSD} > 1\text{ MSD}$, or a warped main scale), never guess with LC formulas! Use the Direct Subtraction Method:

Suppose the main scale mark before $0_V$ is at $x_M$, and the $k^{\text{th}}$ Vernier mark aligns with a main scale mark at position $x_{\text{align}}$:

$$\boxed{\text{Object Length } L = x_{\text{align}} - k \times (1\text{ VSD})}$$

This geometric equation works for 100% of standard, non-standard, and retrograde Vernier Callipers!

Derivation 2: Spherometer Formula for Radius of Curvature R

If $a$ is the distance between the three outer legs of a spherometer and $h$ is the sagittal height by which the central screw is raised/lowered on a curved mirror/lens:

$$\boxed{R = \frac{a^2}{6h} + \frac{h}{2} \approx \frac{a^2}{6h} \quad (\text{for } h \ll a)}$$

topics.jeeTraps:
• Trap 1 (Negative Zero Error Coinciding Division $k$): If a $10$-division Vernier Calliper ($\text{LC} = 0.1\text{ mm}$) has Negative Zero Error and the $7^{\text{th}}$ Vernier division coincides when jaws are closed, the zero error is NOT $-0.7\text{ mm}$! It is $\text{ZE} = -(10 - 7) \times 0.1\text{ mm} = -0.3\text{ mm}$!
  • Trap 2 (Diameter vs. Radius in Wire Volume / Density Error): A Screw Gauge always measures the Diameter ($D$) of a wire, not its radius! Even though $D = 2r$, the relative error is identical: $\frac{\Delta D}{D} = \frac{\Delta r}{r}$.

conclusion: You have mastered Chapter 01: Units, Dimensions and Measurements! You now have the complete toolkit to check any equation dimensionally, propagate experimental errors using calculus, and read any standard or non-standard Vernier Calliper and Screw Gauge.
summary:
• Unit Conversion: $n_1 u_1 = n_2 u_2 \implies n_2 = n_1 [M_1/M_2]^a [L_1/L_2]^b [T_1/T_2]^c$.
  • Homogeneity & Arguments: Added/subtracted terms have identical dimensions; inputs to $\sin, \cos, \exp, \ln$ are strictly $[M^0 L^0 T^0]$.
  • Significant Figures: $+ / -$ keeps least Decimal Places; $\times / \div$ keeps least Total Sig Figs.
  • Error Propagation: For $Z = A^p B^q / C^r$, $\frac{\Delta Z}{Z} = |p|\frac{\Delta A}{A} + |q|\frac{\Delta B}{B} + |r|\frac{\Delta C}{C}$.
  • Instruments: Vernier $\text{LC} = 1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}$; Screw Gauge $\text{LC} = \frac{\text{Pitch}}{N}$; $\text{True Reading} = \text{Observed} - \text{ZE}$.

questions.prompt: How many significant figures are present in the measured quantities (i) $0.005080\text{ m}$, (ii) $6.022 \times 10^{23}$, and (iii) $4200\text{ kg}$?
questions.explanation: (i) Leading zeros are not significant, while trapped and trailing zeros after a decimal point ARE significant ($5, 0, 8, 0 \to \mathbf{4}$). (ii) Powers of 10 are not significant ($6, 0, 2, 2 \to \mathbf{4}$). (iii) Trailing zeros without a decimal point are not significant ($4, 2 \to \mathbf{2}$).

questions.prompt: Round off the following numbers to 3 significant figures using the standard Even–Odd rule: (a) $14.650$, (b) $14.750$, and (c) $14.651$.
questions.explanation: (a) In $14.650$, the dropped digit is $50$ and the preceding digit $6$ is even, so it stays $14.6$. (b) In $14.750$, the preceding digit $7$ is odd, so it rounds up to $14.8$. (c) In $14.651$, $5$ is followed by a non-zero digit $1$, so it must round up to $14.7$.

questions.prompt: Three masses are measured as $m_1 = 12.4\text{ g}$, $m_2 = 3.12\text{ g}$, and $m_3 = 0.084\text{ g}$. What is the total mass $M = m_1 + m_2 + m_3$ reported with proper significant figures?
questions.explanation: Exact sum $= 12.4 + 3.12 + 0.084 = 15.604\text{ g}$. For addition, we round to the least number of decimal places. Since $12.4\text{ g}$ has only 1 decimal place, we round $15.604\text{ g}$ to $15.6\text{ g}$.

questions.prompt: Which of the following pairs of physical quantities does NOT have the same dimensional formula?
options: Surface Tension and Coefficient of Viscosity
questions.answer: Surface Tension and Coefficient of Viscosity
questions.explanation: Surface Tension $[S] = [F/L] = [M^1 L^0 T^{-2}]$, whereas Coefficient of Viscosity $[\eta] = [M^1 L^{-1} T^{-1}]$. All other pairs have identical dimensions!

questions.prompt: The temperatures of two bodies measured by a thermometer are $T_1 = (20 \pm 0.5)^\circ\text{C}$ and $T_2 = (50 \pm 0.5)^\circ\text{C}$. What is the temperature difference $\Delta T = T_2 - T_1$ and its percentage error?
questions.explanation: $\Delta T = 50 - 20 = 30^\circ\text{C}$. Even in subtraction, absolute errors ADD: $0.5 + 0.5 = 1.0^\circ\text{C}$. Percentage error $= \frac{1.0}{30} \times 100\% = 3.33\%$.

questions.prompt: Find the solid angle subtended at the center of a sphere by a conical beam of light whose semi-vertical angle is $\alpha = 60^\circ$.
questions.explanation: Using $\Omega = 2\pi(1 - \cos\alpha)$ with $\alpha = 60^\circ$: $\Omega = 2\pi(1 - \cos 60^\circ) = 2\pi(1 - 1/2) = \pi\text{ sr}$.

questions.prompt: In a standard Vernier Calliper, $1\text{ MSD} = 1\text{ mm}$ and $20$ Vernier scale divisions coincide with $19$ Main scale divisions. What is its Least Count (LC)?
questions.explanation: $\text{LC} = \left(1 - \frac{19}{20}\right) \times 1\text{ mm} = \frac{1}{20}\text{ mm} = 0.05\text{ mm}$ (or $0.005\text{ cm}$).

questions.prompt: The pressure $P$ at depth $z$ depends on distance $x$ and temperature $\theta$ as $P = \frac{\alpha}{\beta} \exp\left(-\frac{\alpha z}{k_B \theta}\right)$, where $k_B$ is Boltzmann's constant. What is the dimensional formula of $\beta$?
questions.explanation: The exponential argument must be dimensionless: $\left[\frac{\alpha z}{k_B \theta}\right] = [M^0 L^0 T^0]$. Since $[k_B \theta] = \text{Energy} = [M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]$, we get $[\alpha] = \frac{[M^1 L^2 T^{-2}]}{[L]} = [M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]$ (Force). Next, $[P] = \left[\frac{\alpha}{\beta}\right] \implies [\beta] = \frac{[\alpha]}{[P]} = \frac{[M^1 L^1 T^{-2}]}{[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]} = [M^0 L^2 T^0]$ (Area!).

questions.prompt: A physical quantity $X$ is given by $X = \frac{a^2 b^3}{c \sqrt{d}}$. If the percentage errors of measurement in $a, b, c,$ and $d$ are $4\%, 2\%, 3\%,$ and $4\%$ respectively, then the maximum percentage error in $X$ is:
If the unit of Force is $100\text{ N}$, the unit of Length is $10\text{ m}$, and the unit of Time is $100\text{ s}$ in a new system of units, what is the unit of Mass in this system?
questions.explanation: From $F = ma = m\frac{L}{T^2}$, we have $[M] = [F^1 L^{-1} T^2]$. Substituting the new units: $1\text{ unit of Mass} = \frac{(100\text{ N})(100\text{ s})^2}{10\text{ m}} = \frac{100 \times 10^4}{10}\text{ kg} = 10^5\text{ kg}$.

questions.prompt: In a simple pendulum experiment, the length of the string is measured as $L = 20.0\text{ cm}$ using a meter scale of accuracy $1\text{ mm}$, and the time for $100$ oscillations is measured as $t = 90\text{ s}$ using a stopwatch of resolution $1\text{ s}$. What is the percentage accuracy in the determination of $g$?
questions.explanation: Since $g = \frac{4\pi^2 L}{T^2}$ and $T = \frac{t}{N}$, $\frac{\Delta g}{g} = \frac{\Delta L}{L} + 2\frac{\Delta t}{t} = \frac{0.1\text{ cm}}{20.0\text{ cm}} + 2\left(\frac{1\text{ s}}{90\text{ s}}\right) = 0.005 + 0.0222 = 0.0272 = 2.72\%$.

questions.prompt: Two resistors $R_1 = (10 \pm 0.5)\,\Omega$ and $R_2 = (10 \pm 0.5)\,\Omega$ are connected in parallel. What is the equivalent resistance $R_p$ with its maximum error limits?
questions.explanation: $R_p = \frac{10 \times 10}{10 + 10} = 5.0\,\Omega$. Using $\Delta R_p = R_p^2\left(\frac{\Delta R_1}{R_1^2} + \frac{\Delta R_2}{R_2^2}\right) = (5)^2\left(\frac{0.5}{100} + \frac{0.5}{100}\right) = 25 \times 0.01 = 0.25\,\Omega$.

questions.prompt: What are the dimensions of the quantity $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}$ and $\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$, where $B$ is magnetic field, $\mu_0$ is permeability, and $\varepsilon_0$ is permittivity of free space?
questions.explanation: $\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} = c$ (speed of light in vacuum), so its dimensions are $[L^1 T^{-1}]$. Meanwhile, $\frac{B^2}{2\mu_0}$ is magnetic energy density (Energy / Volume = Pressure), which has dimensions $[M^1 L^{-1} T^{-2}]$.

questions.prompt: A Screw Gauge has a pitch of $0.5\text{ mm}$ and $50$ divisions on its circular scale. Before starting the measurement, it is found that when the two jaws are brought in contact, the $45^{\text{th}}$ division of the circular scale coincides with the main scale line and the zero of the circular scale lies ABOVE (crosses past) the reference line. What is the Zero Error?
questions.explanation: Least Count $\text{LC} = \frac{0.5\text{ mm}}{50} = 0.01\text{ mm}$. Since the zero of the circular scale has crossed ABOVE the reference line, the zero error is negative: $\text{ZE} = -(N - k) \times \text{LC} = -(50 - 45) \times 0.01\text{ mm} = -0.05\text{ mm}$.

questions.prompt: If speed of light ($c$), gravitational constant ($G$), and Planck's constant ($h$) are chosen as fundamental units, the dimensions of time ($T$) in this Planck system are:
questions.explanation: Let $[T] = [h]^a [G]^b [c]^d = [M^1 L^2 T^{-1}]^a [M^{-1} L^3 T^{-2}]^b [L^1 T^{-1}]^d = [M^{a-b} L^{2a+3b+d} T^{-a-2b-d}]$. Matching exponents: $a - b = 0 \implies a = b$; $-a - 2b - d = 1 \implies d = -3a - 1$; and $2a + 3b + d = 0 \implies 5a + (-3a - 1) = 0 \implies 2a = 1 \implies a = 1/2, b = 1/2, d = -5/2$.

questions.prompt: The density of a solid metal sphere is determined by measuring its mass and its diameter. If the maximum errors in measuring the mass and the diameter are $2\%$ and $1.5\%$ respectively, the maximum error in the calculated density is:
questions.explanation: Volume of a sphere in terms of diameter $D$ is $V = \frac{1}{6}\pi D^3$, so density $\rho = \frac{m}{V} = \frac{6m}{\pi D^3}$. Therefore, $\frac{\Delta \rho}{\rho} \times 100\% = \frac{\Delta m}{m}\times 100\% + 3\left(\frac{\Delta D}{D}\times 100\%\right) = 2\% + 3(1.5\%) = 6.5\%$.

questions.prompt: A customized Vernier Calliper has $1\text{ MSD} = 0.1\text{ cm}$. It is designed such that $10$ divisions of the Vernier scale equal $11$ divisions of the Main scale (a Retrograde Vernier where $1\text{ VSD} = 0.11\text{ cm}$). What is the Least Count (resolution step size) of this Vernier Calliper?
questions.explanation: Here $1\text{ MSD} = 0.10\text{ cm}$ and $1\text{ VSD} = \frac{11}{10}\text{ MSD} = 0.11\text{ cm}$. The resolution step (Least Count) is the absolute difference between one Main Scale division and one Vernier Scale division: $\text{LC} = |1\text{ MSD} - 1\text{ VSD}| = |0.10 - 0.11| = 0.01\text{ cm}$.

questions.prompt: During Searle's method for determining Young's modulus $Y = \frac{4MgL}{\pi d^2 l}$, a student measures the wire diameter $d = 0.4\text{ mm}$ using a Screw Gauge of least count $0.01\text{ mm}$ and the extension $l = 0.8\text{ mm}$ using a Micrometer of least count $0.02\text{ mm}$ ($M, g, L$ are known accurately). Which measurement contributes more to the fractional error in $Y$, and what is the total percentage error in $Y$?
options: Diameter d contributes twice as much as l; Total Error = 7.5%
Both d and l contribute equally; Total Error = 5.0%
Extension l contributes more than d; Total Error = 7.5%
Both d and l contribute equally; Total Error = 7.5%
questions.answer: Diameter d contributes twice as much as l; Total Error = 7.5%
questions.explanation: Since $Y \propto d^{-2} l^{-1}$, we have $\frac{\Delta Y}{Y} = 2\frac{\Delta d}{d} + \frac{\Delta l}{l}$. Contribution from $d$: $2 \times \frac{0.01}{0.4} = 2 \times 0.025 = 0.05 = 5.0\%$. Contribution from $l$: $\frac{0.02}{0.8} = 0.025 = 2.5\%$. Thus $d$ contributes twice as much as $l$, and total error $= 5.0\% + 2.5\% = 7.5\%$.

questions.prompt: In an optics experiment to find the focal length $f$ of a concave mirror using $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{u} + \frac{1}{v}$, a student records object distance $u = (20.0 \pm 0.2)\text{ cm}$ and image distance $v = (20.0 \pm 0.2)\text{ cm}$. What is the percentage error in the calculated focal length $f$?
questions.explanation: First find $f$: $\frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{20} + \frac{1}{20} = \frac{2}{20} \implies f = 10.0\text{ cm}$. Using $\frac{\Delta f}{f^2} = \frac{\Delta u}{u^2} + \frac{\Delta v}{v^2} \implies \frac{\Delta f}{f} = f\left(\frac{\Delta u}{u^2} + \frac{\Delta v}{v^2}\right) = 10\left(\frac{0.2}{400} + \frac{0.2}{400}\right) = 10 \times \frac{0.4}{400} = 0.01 = 1.0\%$.

questions.prompt: There are two Vernier Callipers A and B, both having $1\text{ cm}$ divided into $10$ equal parts on the Main Scale ($1\text{ MSD} = 1\text{ mm}$). In Calliper A, $10\text{ VSD} = 9\text{ MSD}$. In Calliper B, $10\text{ VSD} = 11\text{ MSD}$. While measuring a cylinder, Calliper A has its Vernier zero just past $2.8\text{ cm}$ and the $6^{\text{th}}$ VSD coincides with a main scale mark. In Calliper B, the Vernier zero is also just past $2.8\text{ cm}$ and the $6^{\text{th}}$ VSD coincides with the NEXT main scale mark to the right of $2.8 + 0.6 = 3.4\text{ cm}$ (i.e., at $3.5\text{ cm}$). What are the readings of A and B?
questions.explanation: For standard Calliper A ($\text{LC} = 0.01\text{ cm}$): $L_A = 2.8 + 6(0.01) = 2.86\text{ cm}$. For non-standard Calliper B ($1\text{ VSD} = 0.11\text{ cm}$), use the First-Principles Direct Subtraction Formula: the $6^{\text{th}}$ VSD aligns with the main scale mark at $x_{\text{align}} = 3.50\text{ cm}$. Therefore, the position of the Vernier zero ($L_B$) is $L_B = x_{\text{align}} - 6 \times (1\text{ VSD}) = 3.50\text{ cm} - 6(0.11\text{ cm}) = 3.50 - 0.66 = 2.84\text{ cm}$!
